recall.define: Define process, file descriptor, open file description, zombie process, memory mapping and durability boundary without the glossary, naming the man page or POSIX section that defines each.
recall.distinguish: Give the distinction and a one-line shell or C example for: file descriptor versus open file description; zombie versus orphan; short read versus end of file; exec versus fork; virtual memory versus resident memory.
recall.apply: A parent forks a child after opening a log file, then both write. Using file offset, open file description, close-on-exec and rename-based update, explain why their lines interleave but never overwrite, what changes if the child execs a program that keeps the descriptor, and how to publish a complete replacement of the log atomically.

entries.definition: Creates a child process with inherited process state and separate private memory state. On success it returns the child PID in the parent and zero in the child; on failure no child is created. Duplicated descriptors refer to the same open file descriptions. Copy-on-write is a Linux implementation strategy, not a POSIX requirement; explicitly shared mappings retain their shared contract. Only the calling thread survives in the child of a multithreaded process.
entries.misconception: fork copies the file descriptors as independent files (they share offsets through the open file description).

entries.definition: Replacing the calling process's program image with a new one while keeping the process identity, open descriptors (unless close-on-exec), working directory and signal mask; a successful exec never returns.
entries.misconception: exec starts a new process (it reuses the existing one).

entries.definition: Collecting a terminated child's exit status with wait or waitpid, which releases its process-table entry; until reaped, the terminated child remains a zombie.
entries.misconception: A terminated child disappears on its own (it must be reaped or re-parented to a reaper).

entries.definition: A terminated child whose waitable termination information has not been collected. Most execution resources have been released, but kernel bookkeeping including identity and status remains. It no longer runs and cannot be removed by sending it SIGKILL; the appropriate parent or reaper must collect its status. It is inaccurate to say that it occupies no memory.

distinguish_from.distinction: An orphan is a running child whose parent has exited; it is re-parented to a reaper process. A zombie has exited and awaits reaping.

entries.definition: A process whose parent has terminated before it; the kernel re-parents it to init or a subreaper, which will reap it when it terminates.
entries.misconception: Killing a parent kills its children.

entries.definition: The position in a file at which the next read or write occurs, stored in the open file description and therefore shared by every descriptor duplicated from the same open; pread and pwrite take an explicit offset and leave it unchanged.

authority.locator: DESCRIPTION, opening byte-transfer/offset/EOF and nonblocking rules

entries.misconception: The file offset belongs to the file descriptor.

entries.definition: A descriptor flag (FD_CLOEXEC, set atomically with O_CLOEXEC or SOCK_CLOEXEC) that makes the kernel close the descriptor during exec, preventing leaks of files and sockets into child programs; the flag belongs to the descriptor, not the open file description.
entries.misconception: Setting FD_CLOEXEC after open is race-free in a multithreaded program (another thread may fork in between).

entries.definition: A channel conventionally used as a unidirectional byte stream with read and write descriptors and finite buffering. A read can be short and does not preserve write boundaries; end of file occurs only after buffered data is drained and every write-end reference is closed. PIPE_BUF bounds atomic writes relative to other writers, not total capacity. Blocking and nonblocking calls have different progress/error contracts.

Arranging for a descriptor, commonly standard input/output/error, to refer to a selected open file description. Shell redirections can use open and dup2 before exec; dup2 atomically replaces its destination descriptor. Closing that descriptor first introduces a reuse race if another context can allocate descriptors. Redirection order matters and does not by itself serialize application writes.
entries.misconception: Redirection is a shell feature (it is a descriptor-table operation any program can perform).

entries.definition: Making a region of a file, or anonymous zero-filled memory, appear in the address space with mmap, so that loads and stores replace read and write; a shared mapping writes through to the file and to other processes, a private mapping is copy-on-write.
entries.misconception: A mapped file is loaded into memory by mmap (pages are faulted in on demand).

entries.definition: Storage mapped for shared access by multiple processes, for example a POSIX shared memory object mapped with MAP_SHARED. Mapping the same storage does not provide a synchronization protocol, identical virtual addresses or valid cross-process raw pointers. Initialization, publication, cleanup and process-shared synchronization require explicit contracts. It can avoid copying, but is not universally the fastest IPC.
entries.misconception: Shared memory is synchronized by the kernel (the processes must synchronize it themselves).

entries.definition: Locks on a file or byte range used by cooperating participants to coordinate access. Ordinary advisory locks do not prevent a participant from ignoring them. Traditional process-associated fcntl record locks and flock locks have different inheritance and release rules; closing any descriptor for a file can release that process's traditional record locks. Interaction of lock families depends on platform/filesystem, so noninteraction is not a universal guarantee.
entries.misconception: A file lock prevents other processes from writing.

entries.definition: Replacing a file's contents atomically by writing a temporary file in the same directory, fsyncing it, renaming it over the target and fsyncing the directory; readers see either the old or the new file, never a mixture.

authority.locator: write(2) — RETURN VALUE, ERRORS and NOTES: partial progress, EINTR, EPIPE/SIGPIPE and durability boundary

entries.misconception: rename is durable by itself (the directory entry needs its own fsync).

entries.definition: An execution environment mechanism translating a virtual address space to physical storage with mapping and protection state. The operating system manages mappings and the processor performs target-specific translation and access checks. A valid virtual mapping need not currently have resident backing. Translation caches, page sizes, permissions and faults belong to the target/OS contract, not ISO C.

authority.locator: 9.6, printed pp.849–851: translation and fault path

entries.misconception: A process that mapped 1 GiB uses 1 GiB of RAM.

entries.definition: A per-process soft and hard ceiling (RLIMIT_NOFILE, RLIMIT_STACK, RLIMIT_AS and others) enforced by the kernel; exceeding one turns a normally successful call into an error such as EMFILE, which robust programs must handle.
entries.misconception: Descriptor exhaustion is a bug in the program (it may be the configured limit).

entries.definition: A blocking call that returns -1 with errno set to EINTR because a signal handler ran; the operation did not complete and must be retried, unless the handler was installed with SA_RESTART and the call is one the kernel restarts automatically.

authority.locator: close(2) — NOTES: Dealing with error returns from close() and Linux/POSIX.1-2024 EINTR difference

entries.misconception: Retrying close after EINTR is safe (on Linux the descriptor is already closed).
